messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 18
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Police Officer
  trauma_type: Witnessed domestic violence (childhood)
  pcl5: 77

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Perceived Threat: People acting suspiciously, Tactile (Unexpected Touch): Being touched unprepared
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
  Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind.
  Negative Appraisals: Can't Rely on Self: I can't rely on myself, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Vignette:
Malik, an 18-year-old African American man who had recently started working as a police officer, came to treatment describing a childhood shaped by repeated exposure to violence at home, though the memories that stayed with him were not organized as a clear story. He could call up the events only in brief, separate flashes, each one like a still image. He would describe one moment of his mother backing away near the kitchen table, another of a doorway half open, another of a hand raised in anger, and he said that when these pieces came back, they arrived with the same physical arrangement in his body as they had in the house years earlier. He would stiffen in the chair and sit rigidly, saying that his body felt as if it had gone back into the position it had held then, as though he were again trapped in place and bracing for what came next. When he remembered those episodes, the feeling that followed was not only fear but overwhelming grief, and he spoke quietly about how painful it was to remember that as a child he had no way to stop what was happening.

Over time, Malik had become highly alert to signs that something might go wrong. He was especially unsettled by people acting suspiciously, by the kind of glance or movement that seemed off to him but that he could not easily explain. In his work as a police officer, this meant he found himself scanning every room, hallway, and parking lot for anything that might be used as a weapon or dangerous object. Even in ordinary settings he automatically noticed where a bottle, a heavy tool, or a sharp object was placed, and he said he could not help mentally mapping out what could be used against him or someone else. He also avoided unfamiliar places because, in his words, he could not assess the danger there. If he was sent somewhere new for work, he felt tense before he even got out of the car, and if he had the choice, he preferred routes, buildings, and neighborhoods he already knew. A strange silence affected him strongly as well. He described the moment after noise dropped away as the worst part, because unusual quiet made him feel that something dangerous was about to happen. At work, when a room suddenly went still or a street seemed too calm, he found himself waiting for the next blow. Being touched unprepared was another trigger that upset him sharply. If a coworker tapped his shoulder without warning or someone reached for him before he had time to turn, he would jerk away instinctively, embarrassed by how intense the reaction felt.

These experiences left Malik with a deep distrust of his own ability to handle danger. He had come to believe that he could not rely on himself, because when things had gone wrong in the past he had not been able to stop them. That belief sat alongside a more frightening thought: that the intensity of his reactions since the trauma meant he was going crazy. He watched himself for signs that he was losing control, and when he felt his heart race or his body lock into a tense posture, he worried that something in him was breaking. He also felt haunted by the sense that he could not stop bad things from happening to him. That feeling was particularly strong in settings that were new or quiet, or when he noticed someone lingering too long with a hand hidden or a posture he read as threatening. In those moments, his mind returned not to a full narrative but to those few vivid pictures, each one carrying the same sense of powerlessness.

At home, these patterns had narrowed his life. He was more comfortable staying in known places and felt on edge when plans involved unfamiliar settings, so he often declined invitations or arrived reluctantly and left early. At work, the same vigilance made ordinary tasks exhausting, especially when he had to move through environments where he could not immediately read every person or object. What finally brought him to seek help was that he no longer wanted to keep living as if every quiet room, unfamiliar block, or unexpected touch meant danger was about to strike. He was distressed by how quickly his body reacted and by the conviction that he might be slipping out of control. More than anything, Malik hoped to understand why these memories kept returning in fragments and why his body still seemed to live inside them, and he was afraid that without help he would remain trapped in the same helpless state he had known as a child.
